why: Revisions 1-2 both hard-baked XsAdmissionConfig.turnover_max=150.0 into discovery_reliability_score's rejection logic (a frozen ratio in rev 1, a self-adapting worst-fold statistic in rev 2). On review, the user asked whether turnover_max itself is empirically grounded, or an arbitrary cutoff that could be rejecting genuinely good candidates. Investigation (git log -S on cross_sectional.py, CostModel in contracts.py, and a cross-profile pull of docs/results/*.json) found: (1) no derivation for 150.0 anywhere in this repo -- the introducing commit's docstring cites a 'spec section 3.1' that no longer exists; (2) CostModel is a flat per-fill fee_rate/slippage_rate with no market-impact/liquidity-depth term, so the ledger's cost accounting doesn't get less accurate as turnover rises in any modeled way -- cost_breakeven_min already independently verifies the realized edge clears that flat cost assumption; (3) the actual measured v8_joint point blocked by turnover_max (turnover=175.4x/yr) has the best CAGR (41.1%) of any row across all 10 persisted docs/results/*.json profiles, with a healthy Sharpe (1.46) -- turnover does not empirically predict worse realized economics in this project's own data (the one case with genuinely catastrophic turnover, v3 at 293.6x/yr, is independently attributed by this project's own ADR history to an execution-delay routing bug, not a turnover/cost effect). Hard-baking an unexamined threshold into the search's own rejection criterion is not defensible given this. Revision 3 removes the objective-level rejection entirely and replaces it with non-blocking diagnostic reporting, leaving the actual accept/reject decision at the existing, authoritative evaluate_xs_admission gate (unchanged) plus explicit human review -- and flags turnover_max's own calibration as a separate, out-of-scope follow-up question for the user to decide whether to pursue.

open_follow_up_not_in_scope: Whether XsAdmissionConfig.turnover_max=150.0 is itself well-calibrated is a separate, project-wide empirical question this spec deliberately does not resolve: it would require correlating realized (net-of-cost) OOS Sharpe/CAGR/LCB90 against realized turnover across this project's full historical profile set (a first-pass pull across the 10 current docs/results/*.json files found no clear negative relationship, but N is small and confounded by different weight/leverage choices per profile -- not a rigorous study). If that investigation finds the cap is not predictive of worse realized economics, the more structurally correct fix would be to stop gating on a flat turnover count at all and instead make CostModel's cost accounting genuinely convex in trade frequency (a market-impact/liquidity-depth term) so excessive turnover is organically punished through the P&L it actually causes -- but CostModel is shared platform infrastructure used by every strategy in this codebase, so that change needs its own dedicated spec and explicit user sign-off, never bundled into a feature-scoped change like this one.
